item.title: $3\times10^{-16}$ Stable Laser Deployed on a 4.3 km Mountain
item.description: arXiv:2610.37822v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a transportable stable laser system based on a 10 cm reference cavity and an all-fiber phase-stabilized distribution network for the $^{171}$Yb clock wavelength. We highlight an extended cuboid cavity geometry with 4 times smaller spacer volume than a traditional cubic cavity of the same length [30]. We demonstrate repeatable acceleration sensitivities below $2\times10^{-10}$ g$^{-1}$ in all axes and fractional frequency instability as low as $3 \times 10^{-16}$. We also demonstrate accurate distribution of the stable light over 10 m fibers below the $1\times10^{-18}$ level in an all-fiber optic system. We report the successful deployment of the laser system to the summit of Mount Blue Sky at 4300 m, and for the first time, we report 16-digit laser instability measured outside the lab.
item.dc:creator: Tanner Grogan, Eric Swiler, Tristan Rojo, Tobias Bothwell, Robert J. Fasano, Adam Halaoui, Roger C. Brown, Andrew D. Ludlow

item.title: Cold Hypersonic Gas Jets for Precision Laser Spectroscopy of Radioactive Molecules
item.description: arXiv:2610.38242v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The sensitivity to possible beyond standard model physics via a study of the nuclear Schiff moment (NSM) has since recently been driving laser spectroscopy of short-lived radioactive molecules. These experiments have in part been hindered by inefficient cooling of the molecular degrees of freedom, resulting in complex, difficult to interpret molecular spectra. Hypersonic (de Laval) nozzles have been shown to provide ideal environments to study cold short-lived actinides by means of in-gas-jet laser ionization spectroscopy. We present here the first application of this technique on molecules using $^{229,230,232}$ThO laser ablation targets. Translational and rotational temperatures were characterized via laser spectroscopy and found to be $12.5(25)\,\mathrm{K}$ and $7.2(6)\,\mathrm{K}$, respectively, along the nozzle-collimated $60\,\mathrm{mm}$-long, $5\,\mathrm{mm}$-diameter gas jet. An upper bound of the vibrational temperature was estimated as no transitions from $v''=1$ were observed. Molecular King-plot analysis shows a large field shift of $-4.0(13)\,\mathrm{cm}^{-1}/\mathrm{fm}^2$, indicating enhanced sensitivity to the differential nuclear charge radii. Relativistic FSCCSD calculations reproduce the measured molecular field-shift factor, providing a benchmark between state-of-the-art molecular and atomic calculations.
item.dc:creator: A. Claessens, R. Ferrer, Harshithbabu, L. M. Arndt, Ch. E. D\"ullmann, K. Gaul, F. Ivandikov, G. Neyens, D. Renisch, J. Stricker, W. Saelens, P. Van den Bergh, P. Van Duppen

item.title: Extending the limits of rotationally resolved mid-IR spectroscopy: an accurate model of trioxane derived from combining Fourier transform and sub-Doppler measurements
item.description: arXiv:2610.38565v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: 1,3,5-Trioxane, a polyoxymethylene (POM) molecule relevant to prebiotic chemistry and astrophysics, exhibits a dense rovibrational spectrum that challenges high-resolution spectroscopic characterization. Here, we report an extensive study of its $\nu$ 5 CO symmetric stretching mode (960-1000 cm -1 ) by combining broadband high-resolution FTIR spectroscopy (0.001 cm -1 resolution, >2000 transitions) with SI-traceable sub-Doppler saturated absorption measurements using frequency-stabilized CO 2 lasers and a frequency-comb-referenced quantum cascade laser. The latter achieve lineposition uncertainties as low as 40 kHz, revealing inaccuracies in the FTIR frequency scale. A frequency-scale correction is determined by maximizing the global consistency of the complete spectroscopic data set. A global least-squares Hamiltonian fit combining the calibrated FTIR data, the SI-traceable sub-Doppler measurements and previously reported millimeter-wave rotational transitions yields a refined spectroscopic model. The resulting analysis significantly improves the precision of the rotational, quartic, and sextic constants for both the ground and $\nu$ 5 excited vibrational states. This work extends mid-infrared frequency metrology to the largest molecule studied to date (12 atoms), providing a dense set of reference transitions for frequency calibration around 970 cm -1 . The resulting spectroscopic parameters reach relative uncertainties as low as 3.7 x 10 -10 for the band origin, making them valuable for molecular databases used in astrophysics and atmospheric physics, as well as for precision measurements in fundamental physics. Additionally, the observed line shapes indicate the absence of significant intramolecular vibrational energy redistribution (IVR) within the investigated energy range, while a few discrepancies in the Hamiltonian fit suggest the onset of weak perturbations, demonstrating the sensitivity of the present approach to probe subtle intramolecular couplings in complex polyatomic spectra. Q P (31,10) 28 967 426 394.

item.title: Light and charge yields from nuclear recoils in noble liquids: From sub-keV energies to 1 MeV
item.description: arXiv:2610.38718v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a first-principles study of total quanta and charge recombination in noble liquids, based on a solution of Lindhard's integro-differential equation for atomic motion with electronic straggling and detailed modeling of inter-atomic potentials. We introduce the electronic scaling length $\xi_e$ as a fundamental parameter related to a physical observable of the system. We study the energy and electric-field dependence of the exciton-to-ion ratio for nuclear recoils based on the Bates-Griffing process and semiclassical atomic interactions. The resulting light and charge yields are expressed through the recombination probability in the Thomas-Imel box model using the calculated parameter $\xi_e$ and one fitted constant. We compare our model with recent measurements of the electric-field dependence of the box size in LAr and LXe and provide a physical explanation for this behavior. Our model extends to sub-keV energies and provides a consistent description of available data from a few keV to 1 MeV, yielding better overall agreement with existing LAr data than NEST and offering predictions for LXe.
item.dc:creator: Y. Sarkis, Juan Carlos D'Olivo, Alexis Aguilar-Arevalo

item.title: Theoretical Study of Classical Dynamics of Electron in Two-Frequency Paul Trap
item.description: arXiv:2610.38936v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a theoretical study of trapping an electron in a two-frequency Paul trap, motivated by future hybrid architecture consisting of a doubly charged calcium ion (Ca$^{2+}$) and an electron. By isolating the electron from ionic-electron interactions, we formulate the equations of motion for the electron in the time-dependent trap potentials and cast them in the Hill form. Stability and dynamics are then analysed in terms of the dimensionless q-parameters, which encode the applied voltages, drive frequencies, trap geometry, and the particle's charge-to-mass ratio. Under the combined action of the two radio-frequency fields, the trapped electron's classical motion is shown to be approximated well by a slow secular oscillation modulated by two distinct motion sidebands originating from the low- and high-frequency RF drives. The approximation method presented here enables a quick evaluation of the relation between the device-design q-parameters and the electron motion. It offers a crucial foundation for developing physical models of electron-ion interactions in electron-ion traps.

item.title: Simultaneous SI-traceable measurement of the amplitude and the ellipticity of microwave fields with cold Rydberg atoms
item.description: arXiv:2610.39921v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a method for the simultaneous measurement of the amplitude and the ellipticity of microwave fields using trap-loss spectroscopy based on Rydberg excitation of a cold ensemble of 87Rb atoms. The measurement consists of probing the energy spectrum of the $61S_{1/2}$ to $61P_{1/2}$ transition in the presence of microwave, which depends on the electric field amplitude $|E|$ and the third Stokes parameter $|S_3|$. We use a millimeter-size magneto-optical trap to perform strongly-localized measurements, which mitigates the effect of microwave field inhomogeneities. This allows us to work with large Rabi frequencies and thus resolve small deviations from linear or circular states of polarization. Taking into account the effect of non-resonant couplings to neighboring Rydberg states, we measure $|E|$ and $|S_3|$ with an accuracy on the order of 1 percent in the Autler-Townes regime where the measurements can be traced to the international system of units. By studying the visibility of the spectral features as a function of the polarization of the excitation laser beams, we extract some information on the angle of arrival of the microwave field onto the atoms, with good agreement between theory and experiment.
item.dc:creator: Anthony El Bekai, Romain Granier, Miguel Angel Cifuentes Marin, C\'edric Blanchard, Nassim Zahzam, Yannick Bidel, Alexandre Bresson, Alexis Bonnin, Sylvain Schwartz

item.title: High-Fidelity Universal Quantum Gates in a Cryogenic Atom Array
item.description: arXiv:2610.40329v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Neutral atoms in optical tweezer arrays have emerged as a leading platform for quantum information processing. The fidelity of entangling gates mediated by Rydberg interactions has improved rapidly and is increasingly constrained by blackbody-radiation-induced transitions, which shorten Rydberg lifetimes and create contaminant states that can cause correlated errors. Cryogenic environments can suppress these transition rates by more than an order of magnitude. However, realizing a universal gate set in such an environment has remained an outstanding challenge. Here, we demonstrate a universal quantum gate set in a cryogenic $^{133}$Cs atom array, with a single-qubit gate fidelity of 99.970(2)% and a raw two-qubit entangling-gate fidelity of 99.76(8)%, within the range of leading room-temperature implementations. The entangling gate uses direct single-photon coupling between the electronic ground state and a Rydberg $P$ state, avoiding scattering and light shifts associated with two-photon coupling. The gate operates at a modest Rabi frequency of $2\pi\times4.3$ MHz. The measured fidelity agrees with our error model dominated by atomic motion, indicating a straightforward route to higher fidelity through improved cooling, while the fundamental error contribution from Rydberg decay is below $3\times10^{-4}$. These results establish a path to entangling-gate fidelities substantially beyond the current state of the art through cryogenic suppression of Rydberg decay, reducing the overhead for fault-tolerant computation.
item.dc:creator: Junlan Jin, Donghyuk Seo, Yue Shi, Yukai Lu, Jeff D. Thompson, Waseem S. Bakr

item.title: Ionization and Dissociation Energies of Molecular Hydrogen
item.description: arXiv:2610.40359v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Molecular hydrogen (H$_2$) is the simplest neutral molecule and its ionization and dissociation energies are key benchmarks for testing first-principles calculations of nonadiabatic, relativistic, quantum-electrodynamic and finite-nuclear-size effects in molecules. To obtain improved H$_2$ ionization and dissociation energies, we performed precision measurements of 15 transition frequencies in para-H$_2$. They connect the X $^1\Sigma_g^+(v=0,N=0)$ ground state, the long-lived EF $^1\Sigma_g^+(v=0,N=0)$ excited state, and several high members of the $n$p and $n$d Rydberg series with principal quantum number $n$ in the range between 48 and 70. The new data by itself leads to a five times more accurate value of the ionization energy of the ground state of para-H$_2$, equivalent to a relative frequency accuracy of $5\times 10^{-11}$. Combined with a global network analysis of 45 energy intervals in para- and ortho-H$_2$ that have been measured in the past three decades, we obtain new statistically robust values for the ionization energy [$E_{\rm I}(0,0)/(hc)= 124\,417.491\,1573(58)$~cm$^{-1}$] and the dissociation energy [$D_0^{N=0}=36\,118.069\,6646(58)$~cm$^{-1}$] of H$_2$. These values have an unprecedented accuracy equivalent to 175 kHz. The network analysis also leads to improved term values and dissociation energies of the excited states involved in the analysis. By comparing the results with first-principles calculations of the level structures of H$_2$ and H$_2^+$ , a significantly reduced upper bound of 540 kHz is derived for putative beyond-the-standard-model contributions to the energy difference between para- and ortho-H$_2$.

item.title: Tan's Contact for Trapped Spin-Orbit-Coupled Fermi Gases at Finite Temperature
item.description: arXiv:2610.38512v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Tan's contact, bridging microscopic features of many-body quantum systems to two-body contact interactions, is pivotal in the description of quantum gases. However, past studies of Tan's contact of the spin-orbit coupled Fermi gases have been exclusively discussed at zero temperature. The thermal effects on that, which cannot be neglected in most experimental conditions, has not been explored so far. Here, through a path integral Monte Carlo (PIMC) study, we show that thermal effects fundamentally alter the scaling relation between spin-orbit coupling (SOC) and Tan's contact. The linear scaling of Tan's contact with respect to the strength of SOC found at zero temperature is drastically undermined by the thermal effects. And a new mechanism based on the competition between the mean occupancy and the energy-reweighted occupancy of the opposite spin fermion pairs within the interaction range has been unveiled, which radically changes the above linear scaling to a non-monotonic dependence. Our work should be useful for future experiments to explore the preternatural thermal effects on Tan's contact of the strongly interacting spin-orbit-coupled Fermi gas.
item.dc:creator: Tianhao Wu, Yuanbang Wei, Rui Tian, Dongdong Pu, Beizhi Chen, Qihang Ying, Hongyan Shi, Yue Zhang, Shuai Li, Bo Liu

item.title: Gravitational Interactions in Nuclear Clocks
item.description: arXiv:2610.38832v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Atomic clocks achieve extraordinary precision through quantum control over large ensembles of atoms, with precision increasing and atom number advancing steadily. Emerging nuclear clock technology encodes clock states in nuclear rather than electronic transitions, offering a new frontier for precision measurement. Here we study whether a large ensemble of such clock nuclei could be used to observe their mutual gravitational interaction. We investigate the gravitational redshift induced by neighboring atoms, including nuclear energy superpositions as sources of gravity, giving rise to a genuinely quantum gravitational interaction between pairs of nuclei. We find that the resulting clock frequency shift due to mutual gravity may become non-negligible for a macroscopic number of nuclei, for instance in a solid-state thorium clock, and we propose approaches to mitigate electromagnetic field effects by exploiting spatial symmetry and high-precision spectroscopy. We further discuss how energy-induced mass superpositions could be directly probed using external gravitational field sensors. By contrast, observing gravity-induced entanglement involving clocks would require substantially greater experimental advances due to decoherence from spontaneous emission. Taken together, our results suggest that nuclear clocks, either alone or in combination with complementary sensors such as optomechanical systems, may offer a future route toward probing gravity at short distances and testing gravitating quantum source masses beyond the Newtonian limit.
item.dc:creator: Konstantin Beyer, Niklas E. \"Onne, Shimon Kolkowitz, Dolev Bluvstein, Mikhail Lukin, Jun Ye, Igor Pikovski

item.title: Reverse Quantum Annealing for Ground-State Energy Calculation in Molecule
item.description: arXiv:2610.39129v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We present the results of our reverse quantum annealing computations of the ground-state energies of alkaline-earth monofluoride molecules. By partitioning the Dirac--Coulomb electronic Hamiltonian into sub-QUBOs and refining forward-annealing solutions through optimized reverse-annealing schedules, residual configuration errors are systematically minimized. The electronic ground-state wave functions and energies are obtained using the Quantum Annealing Eigensolver algorithm. This work provides a pathway for achieving sub-milliHartree chemical accuracy and advancing molecular electronic structure calculations in the quantum annealing paradigm.
item.dc:creator: Pradyot Pritam Sahoo

item.title: Optical clock network tracks tidal variations of the gravity potential
item.description: arXiv:2610.39635v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Gravity affects the passage of time, as described by General Relativity. On Earth, the rate of a clock as seen by a fixed observer changes by about one part in $10^{16}$ per metre in height. Chronometric levelling exploits this effect to directly measure differences in gravity potential by comparing distant clocks. It has been proposed as a complementary approach to established geodetic techniques for linking height reference systems and monitoring the terrestrial gravity potential. Experimental demonstrations have to date focused primarily on static potential differences. Yet, the potentials of the Moon, the Sun and other celestial bodies as well as the Earth's response to their tidal forcing change clock rates by several $10^{-17}$, providing a predictable test signal to demonstrate optical clock networks resolving small variations in relativistic time dilation. Here, we report chronometric observations of time-varying gravity potential differences using a network of optical clocks and phase-stabilized fibre links in Europe. Two distinct geographical configurations, with baselines of about 800 km each, result in different combinations of diurnal and semidiurnal tidal components. One comparison uses a transportable optical clock as a remote sensor. The measured rate shifts track the tidal variations, resolving the predicted signal within 1 d of measurement and agreeing with model predictions. These results extend experimental chronometric levelling from static to dynamic potential differences and highlight the need to account for the time dependence of relativistic time dilation in frequency metrology. They also open the prospect for quantum clock networks with improved stability and availability to move beyond known tides and monitor other gravity potential variations, such as those arising from surface deformation and mass redistribution in geologically or volcanically active regions.

item.title: Kelvin-Wave Multiplication by Sound Emission
item.description: arXiv:2610.39909v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A subsonic Kelvin quantum can emit a phonon and split into two softer quanta, increasing Kelvin population while losing energy. In the soft-phonon limit, rotational invariance relates the leading acoustic shear amplitude, odd under reversal of phonon axial momentum, to the energy released. Microscopic calculations support this dispersion dependence. In a reflecting cavity with coherent sound and Kelvin seeds, Gross--Pitaevskii evolution shows Kelvin gain, larger mean-square displacement and smaller mean-square slope; a $\pi$ shift of the initial sound phase reverses these changes.
item.dc:creator: Weican Yang

item.title: Resolving Photochemical Reaction Pathways Using Field-Induced Surface Hopping Simulation of fs-EUV-TRPES: The Case of Furan
item.description: arXiv:2610.40011v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Recent advances in femtosecond extreme ultraviolet photoelectron spectroscopy have enabled insight into photochemistry in gases, condensed phases, and at interfaces. Assigning spectral features to reaction pathways requires theoretical predictions connecting nonadiabatic dynamics to measured observables. Here, we present a general approach for resolving photochemical reaction pathways by combining field-induced surface hopping with explicit pulse excitation, RMS-CASPT2, and simulations of time-resolved photoelectron spectra. The pump field prepares the excited-state ensemble under experimental conditions, while the multireference treatment describes excited states, conical intersections, and bond-breaking coordinates. Mapping trajectories onto photoelectron signals, supported by a systematic analysis of photoionization approximations, enables comparison with experiment. We apply this approach to furan excited by a 200 nm, 10 fs pulse. Among trajectories returning to the ground state, approximately 87 % hop near the ring-puckering conical intersection and 13 % near the ring-opening intersection. Subsequent ground-state vibrational energy redistribution nevertheless populates ring-opening structures. Five ground-state products are identified. Simulated spectra reproduce time-dependent electron-binding-energy shifts, characteristic kinks, and bands with predicted photoproduct contributions. Compared with Dyson-norm-based intensities, plane- and Coulomb-wave continuum functions improve the early-time shape of the lowest binding energy signal and show that photoelectron anisotropy is more sensitive to the continuum approximation than the angle-integrated spectrum. More generally, these findings demonstrate how explicit-pulse nonadiabatic dynamics and dynamically correlated multireference electronic structure can resolve competing photochemical reaction pathways through simulated fs-EUV-TRPES.
item.dc:creator: Xincheng Miao, Toshinori Suzuki, Roland Mitri\'c

item.title: Single-atom billiards in an ultracold bath with energy-tunable collisions and threshold-sensitive detection
item.description: arXiv:2610.40098v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Transport processes at the microscopic scale can differ strongly from their macroscopic counterparts, particularly when the environment is not a well-defined surface but an unordered thermal medium. Ultracold quantum gases offer a high degree of controllability and directly observable dynamics, thereby providing a versatile platform to study such transport processes under precisely controllable conditions. Here, we realize an energy-tunable single-atom collider by transporting individual cesium atoms at controlled velocity through an ultracold rubidium bath. The constant lattice velocity sets the directed contribution to the collision-energy distribution, while the lattice depth provides a tunable energy threshold for collision-induced transport disruption. By independently varying these parameters together with bath density and temperature, we separate the number of collision events from their probability to disrupt transport. Across a regime with only a few expected collisions per passage, the inferred single-collision ejection probability rises from small values to near unity as the collision energy exceeds the lattice confinement scale. The experiment thus converts microscopic collisional energy transfer into a binary single-atom observable and provides a controlled link between individual scattering events and emergent dissipative transport.
item.dc:creator: Silvia Hiebel, Sabrina Burgardt, Julian Fe{\ss}, Artur Widera

item.title: Static dipolar impurity in a Fermi gas
item.description: arXiv:2610.40460v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We consider a static dipolar impurity immersed in a Fermi gas and show how dipolar interactions shape both the few-body scattering properties and the resulting polaron physics. Using Fumi's theorem, we connect the anisotropic phase shifts directly to the ground-state energy, and compute the exact impurity spectrum via the functional determinant approach. The resulting spectrum is a convolution of independent even- and odd-wave contributions, giving rise to a ground state with simultaneously occupied even- and odd-wave bound states whose separation is tunable via the dipole length. A variational ansatz limited to one particle-hole excitation fails to capture this doubly occupied ground state. We further find that long-range dipolar interactions weaken Anderson's orthogonality catastrophe, reducing the power-law decay of the quasiparticle weight. These effects can be tested with ultracold polar molecules, where microwave shielding and independent tunability of interactions enable experimental access to the predicted regimes.
item.dc:creator: Eugen Dizer, Xin Chen, Richard Schmidt, Arthur Christianen

item.title: Exceptional Points as Witnesses of Non-Gaussian Noise
item.description: arXiv:2610.40612v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Efficient control of quantum devices requires the knowledge of their environmental noise, yet the commonly measured power spectrum does not fully characterize non-Gaussian fluctuations of realistic environments. Here we show that exceptional points (EPs) in the noise-averaged dephasing response can expose observable signatures of non-Gaussian statistics, distinguishing environments with identical lower-order statistics. We also introduce a theoretical model that describes dephasing environments in terms of identical independent noise sources while preserving the power spectrum. Given a calibrated single-source model, the largest EP order extracted from the measured dephasing response determines the number of sources and predicts the higher-order statistics of the combined noise. We illustrate an atomtronic readout that maps distinct EP signatures onto an evolving ensemble-averaged atomic interference pattern. Our results connect non-Hermitian dynamics to environmental noise statistics, providing a route to characterize noise in quantum devices used in computing, metrology, and precision measurement.
item.dc:creator: Aritra Ghosh, Subhashish Banerjee, M. Bhattacharya

item.title: Precision Isotope-Shift Measurement of the ${}^1S_0 \leftrightarrow {}^3P_2$ Transition and a Multi-Transition King-Plot Consistency Test
item.description: arXiv:2601.08487v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present precision spectroscopy and isotope shift measurement of the ${}^1S_0 \leftrightarrow {}^3P_2$ clock transition in neutral ytterbium ($\mathrm{Yb}$) atoms. By revealing a magic wavelength at $905.4(2)$ nm, we successfully achieve the atomic spectrum narrower than $100$ Hz. The interleaved clock operation between isotopes allows us to determine isotope shifts of four bosonic isotope pairs at Hz-level uncertainties, which is combined with those of other four ultra-narrow transitions in $\mathrm{Yb}$ and $\mathrm{Yb}^+$ to construct the King plot. We show that a rich dataset spanning multiple transitions enables a test of a restricted isotope-shift ansatz comprising the leading mass and field shifts, one effective factorized higher-order Standard Model contribution, and a new-particle contribution. Within this ansatz, the five-transition data are inconsistent with the new-particle contribution serving as the sole additional contribution over the mass ranges $m_\phi \leq 6.5$ keV and $18$ keV $\leq m_\phi < 100$ keV, while the previous works rely on another bound set by the neutron scattering and $(g-2)_e$ measurements. This work paves the way for the effective use of precision isotope shift data in the King plot analysis and stimulates further measurements in Yb and other elements.
item.dc:creator: Taiki Ishiyama, Koki Ono, Reiji Asano, Hokuto Kawase, Tetsushi Takano, Ayaki Sunaga, Yasuhiro Yamamoto, Minoru Tanaka, Yoshiro Takahashi

item.title: Isotopic effect on collisional widths and shifts of Hg clock transition induced by cold Rb atoms
item.description: arXiv:2605.01908v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study the isotopic dependence of collisional widths and shifts of the Hg clock transition $^1$S$_0$-$^3$P$_0$ perturbed by the Rb atoms in the temperature range from 1 nK to 1 K. For this purpose, we model the Born-Oppenheimer effective interaction potential by including the leading long-range van der Waals coefficients. For elastic collisions, we show the connection between the dependence of collision line shape parameters on the reduced mass of colliding partners as well as the variation of the scattering length in the excited and ground states of the Hg-Rb system in the $\upmu$K temperature range. We confront the full quantum scattering calculations with a semi-classical approximation for collisional widths and shifts. We show that the shape resonances in excited and ground scattering states lead to significant variations of collisional line shape parameters with the change of the reduced mass of colliding atoms. We also indicate the possible influence of inelastic collisions, which could lead to universal behavior and significantly affect the dependence of collisional broadening and shifting on the isotopic combination of colliding atoms.
item.dc:creator: Renu Bala, Adam Linek, Marcin Witkowski, Piotr S. \.Zuchowski, Micha{\l} Zawada, Paul S. Julienne, Roman Ciury{\l}o

item.title: Enhanced coherence of rare-earth nuclear spins in a crystal
item.description: arXiv:2608.03939v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Rare-earth ions in crystals are useful in precision measurements and quantum information science because of their exceptional optical and spin coherence properties. We show that the nuclear spin coherence time of $^{153}\mathrm{Eu}^{3+}$ ions doped into yttrium orthosilicate can be significantly enhanced by driving the environmental nuclear spins in the host crystal. This method of enhancing the spin coherence time can lead to improved precision measurements using rare-earth-doped crystals.
item.dc:creator: Bassam Nima, Yuiki Takahashi, Amar Vutha

item.title: Long-Baseline Phase-Coherent Microwave Reception Using Rydberg Atoms
item.description: arXiv:2610.33552v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A long baseline phase-coherent microwave receiver is demonstrated using a remotely interrogated cesium Rydberg atom sensor over an 8 m free-space optical link. A 3.989 GHz local oscillator (LO) is intensity-modulated onto an 852 nm optical probe and recovered remotely for atomic superheterodyne detection. A 509 nm coupling laser establishes a Rydberg electromagnetically induced transparency (EIT) system addressing the 6S1/2 to 6P3/2 to 56D5/2 ladder, with microwave coupling to 57P3/2. A test signal offset by 5 kHz generates an optically detected intermediate-frequency (IF) response returned to the reference station for centralized coherent acquisition. This eliminates independent remote oscillators, electronic IF acquisition, and distributed clock synchronization. Over 10 min, the differential phase between remote and local reference exhibits a standard deviation of 0.476 deg and a minimum overlapping phase Allan deviation of 0.048 deg at approximately 200 s averaging. Following optical-link interruption, the differential phase recovers without recalibration, with a measured pre- and post-interruption difference of 0.01 deg. These results demonstrate phase coherent remotely interrogated atomic microwave reception with reduced instrumentation, supporting future distributed interferometry, multistatic radar, and coherent sensor arrays.
item.dc:creator: Darmindra Arumugam, Brook Feyissa

item.title: Decay versus dephasing in Rydberg analog optimization: the exchange rate depends on the readout
item.description: arXiv:2608.29858v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Numerical studies of noisy Rydberg-atom optimization compress decoherence into a single rate, treating spontaneous decay ($\Gamma$) and dephasing ($\gamma$) as equivalent. We resolve the two as independent Lindblad axes for quantum annealing of unit-disk maximum independent set at fixed annealing time and ask how their relative effect depends on the readout. For the raw readout the size error collapses onto the effective dephasing rate $u=\kappa\Gamma+\gamma$, and at small noise a unit of decay rate degrades the result as much as $\kappa=7.4$ units of dephasing rate; a collapse fit across the whole grid returns 8.3. After greedy completion followed by a $(1,2)$-swap local search, classical post-processing of polynomial cost, the exchange rate falls to $\kappa=1.6$, and at the calibrated operating point of a commercial device dephasing produces three quarters of the noise-induced error instead of two fifths. First-order perturbation theory built from noiseless propagation gives the decay and dephasing susceptibilities of every readout, raw or post-processed, to a few parts in $10^6$ of the full Lindblad result. The raw asymmetry is set at the end of the schedule, where a decay event deletes an atom and a dephasing event leaves the readout unchanged. Post-processing refills most deletions and leaves misplaced atoms, which the two channels produce at comparable rates. Which channel limits a device therefore depends on the readout as well as on the hardware.
item.dc:creator: Seunghyeon Kim, Minju Kim, Junwoo Jung

item.title: Geometry-controlled zeros of resonant Kelvin-wave conversion in four spatial dimensions
item.description: arXiv:2610.29218v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We show that geometry can suppress resonant four-wave conversion of Kelvin waves on a vortex surface in four spatial dimensions. Perpendicular incoming waves eliminate the entire local-area contribution, exposing a finite interaction mediated by the surrounding fluid. Reflection allows the incoming wave-number ratio to vary at exact resonance, revealing a sign-changing zero of this fluid coupling at \(\lambda_*\simeq1.469\). Uniform matching of the Gross--Pitaevskii (GP) four-wave coupling to the fluid result establishes microscopic zeros that approach this ratio at long wavelengths. Numerical calculations also show the corresponding sign change. Independent calculations in separate resonant geometries connect the coupling sign to the phase of coherently generated waves and the frequency ordering of reflection-even and reflection-odd modes. The surrounding flow thus determines whether an exactly resonant conversion channel is present at four-wave order.
